mechanism: Diagnostic accuracy is biased when receipt of the reference standard depends on the index-test result, so disease status is verified in a nonrandom subset of tested participants.
vignette: Investigators prospectively enroll consecutive adults being evaluated for coronary artery disease and perform a new blood-based index test on every participant. Coronary angiography is the single prespecified reference standard. All participants with a positive index test undergo angiography, but because angiography is invasive, only a small random sample of participants with a negative index test undergo it. Sensitivity and specificity are then estimated only from participants whose disease status was verified by angiography. Angiographers are blinded to the index-test result.
lead: Which source of bias most directly threatens the reported diagnostic accuracy?
distractor_notes: Spectrum bias arises when the included patient spectrum does not represent the population in which the test will be used. The study instead enrolls consecutive clinically relevant patients; the defining defect is selective application of the reference standard.

Differential verification bias occurs when different reference standards are used for different participants, often according to the index-test result. Here, coronary angiography is the only reference standard; the problem is that many index-negative participants are not verified at all.

Incorporation bias occurs when the index-test result forms part of the reference standard used to define disease. Here, angiography is prespecified independently and does not incorporate the blood-test result.
Reference-standard review bias occurs when interpretation of the reference standard is influenced by knowledge of the index test. The angiographers are explicitly blinded.
key_expl: This study has partial verification bias, also called workup bias. Whether a participant receives the reference standard depends strongly on the index-test result: nearly all index-positive participants are verified, whereas most index-negative participants are not. Disease status is therefore known in a nonrandom subset of the tested cohort, which can bias estimated sensitivity and specificity.
objective: Recognize partial verification bias in diagnostic-accuracy studies when the likelihood of receiving the reference standard depends on the index-test result.

sources.title: Studies of diagnostic test accuracy: Partial verification bias and test result-based sampling
sources.support: The PubMed-indexed methods paper states that partial verification bias occurs when a positive index test makes application of the reference standard more likely and explains that using definitive verification selectively can distort evaluation of diagnostic-test usefulness.
